history.reaction: Corn stocks printed 2.095 billion bushels — above the entire pre-report trade range (1.843–2.005B), not just the 1.918B average. A real miss: more old-crop corn was sitting in bins and elevators on September 1 than any surveyed analyst had guessed.
Soybean stocks printed 0.315 billion bushels — under the 0.324B trade average and inside the survey's 0.304–0.349B range, but far enough below average to score bullish rather than in line.

Wheat stocks printed 1.846 billion bushels. No trade estimate was on file to grade this against — the only survey found had a wheat figure that didn't reconcile against a cited WASDE number, so it was withheld rather than published. The print stands on the record; it just isn't scored.

USDA's first survey-based corn yield came in at 180.7 — 2.3 under July and 1.3 under the trade's 182.0. More acres (planted up 1.4M to 96.7M) kept production near-record at 16.013B bu, but the market traded the yield cut and the 1.653B carryout (down from 1.79B): December corn settled up 15 cents at $4.78.

Soybean yield printed 52.7 — a couple tenths under both July and the trade, effectively in line. The acreage add (planted up 1.4M to 86.8M) still makes 4.519B bu the largest soybean crop on record, and carryout ticked up to 320M. November beans settled up 12 cents at $11.84, riding corn's coattails more than their own numbers.

The report's one real surprise: new-crop wheat carryout cut to 744M — 21M below the trade and 18M under May — on a smaller Hard Red Winter crop (all-wheat production trimmed to 1,543M, yield 47.0). Bullish wheat; farm price cut $0.50 to $6.00.
